# The Length of the Coast

In the 1950s, an English Quaker named Lewis Fry Richardson was trying to answer a question about war. He had a theory, reasonable on its face, that the probability of two countries fighting each other might relate to the length of the border they shared. More border, more friction, more chances for a dispute over a river or a village or a grazing field to curdle into something worse. It was the kind of hypothesis you could test, if you had the numbers. So he went looking for the numbers.

What he found was that nobody agreed on them. Spain reported its border with Portugal as 987 kilometers. Portugal reported the same border as 1,214 kilometers. The Netherlands and Belgium disagreed about theirs by a similarly embarrassing margin. These weren't disputed borders in the political sense. Nobody was arguing about where the line was. They were arguing, without knowing it, about how long a line is.

Richardson noticed something that should have been obvious and somehow wasn't: the smaller the country, the longer it tended to report its shared border. A small nation surveys its frontier carefully, with a fine instrument, following every bend. A large nation measures its many borders with a coarser ruler, stepping over the little wiggles. And the finer your ruler, the longer the border gets. Not a little longer. Systematically, unboundedly longer. Measure the coast of Britain with a 200-kilometer stick and you get one number. Measure it with a 50-kilometer stick and you get a much larger one, because now you're following bays you used to skip across. Measure it with a meter stick and you're tracing the edges of individual rocks. Measure it with a centimeter and you're going around pebbles.

There is no bottom to this. The coastline doesn't converge on a true length the way a circle's perimeter does when you inscribe polygons with more and more sides. It just keeps growing.

Richardson published this observation in a fairly obscure place, and it would have stayed there if Benoit Mandelbrot hadn't found it. In 1967 Mandelbrot wrote a short paper in *Science* called "How Long Is the Coast of Britain?" and used Richardson's data to introduce an idea he would spend the rest of his career developing: that some shapes have a dimension that isn't a whole number. A smooth line is one-dimensional. A filled-in plane is two-dimensional. The west coast of Britain, by Richardson's measurements, is about 1.25-dimensional: more than a line, less than a surface, a thing that crumples into space without ever filling it. The answer to "how long is the coast?" is not a number. It's a relationship between the length you get and the ruler you use.

---

I find this story moving in a way that's a little hard to justify. Part of it is Richardson himself, who deserves to be better known. He was a physicist and mathematician who, during the First World War, served as an ambulance driver with the Friends' Ambulance Unit in France, because his Quaker convictions wouldn't let him fight but also wouldn't let him stay home. In the intervals between ferrying wounded men, in a rest billet he described as a "heap of hay in a cold rest billet," he worked out by hand a numerical weather forecast. It was the first serious attempt to predict the weather by solving the equations of the atmosphere directly, rather than by looking at today's map and remembering what usually happened next.

It took him something like six weeks of calculation to produce a forecast for a six-hour period. And the forecast was wildly wrong: he predicted a pressure change of 145 hectopascals over six hours, which is not a weather event so much as the end of the world. Decades later, the meteorologist Peter Lynch showed that Richardson's method was essentially sound; the problem was in his starting data, which contained small noisy fluctuations that the equations amplified into nonsense. Smooth the data first, and Richardson's hand calculation gives a reasonable answer. He was right, and he had been wrong only in the way a person is wrong when they are the first to try something and nobody yet knows where the traps are.

In his 1922 book on the subject, Richardson imagined a "forecast factory": an enormous spherical hall, its walls painted with a map of the globe, filled with 64,000 human computers, each responsible for calculating the weather in their small patch of the world. A conductor in the center would shine colored lights on the regions running ahead or behind, keeping the whole thing synchronized, like an orchestra playing the atmosphere. It's one of the most beautiful images in the history of science, and it's also an almost exact description of how weather forecasting works now, except the computers are silicon and the hall is a server room.

Then, in the 1920s, the Meteorological Office where he worked was absorbed into the Air Ministry. Richardson understood that better weather forecasting would mean better aerial bombing. He left. He went back to studying the causes of war, trying to find mathematical regularities in the history of human conflict, which is how he came to be counting the length of borders in the first place. He was trying to make peace a science. Along the way he tripped over fractals and didn't quite realize what he'd found.

---

But the bigger reason the coastline paradox moves me is that it seems to be about much more than coastlines.

The lesson isn't that coastlines are unmeasurable. You can measure them fine. The lesson is that the measurement is a joint product of the thing and the instrument, and for some kinds of things, you cannot pull the two apart. Ask "how long is the coast?" and the honest answer is "at what resolution?" There isn't a hidden, true, ruler-independent length waiting behind the numbers. The dependence on scale *is* the fact about the coastline.

Once you start looking, this pattern turns up everywhere.

How many things happened to you yesterday? At the coarsest resolution, one thing: you had a day. At a finer one, a few: you worked, you ate, you talked to someone, you slept. Finer still and you're into dozens, then hundreds, each conversation breaking into exchanges and each exchange into sentences and each sentence into the moment you chose one word instead of another. There is no correct count. There's only the count you get when you decide how closely to look.

How long is a piece of music? The clock says four minutes. But anyone who has heard a piece they love knows it has a different length depending on how you're listening: a song on in the background while you cook passes in a blink, and the same song heard with full attention, noticing where the bass line moves and how the singer's breath catches before the bridge, feels like it contains whole rooms. The four minutes is the 200-kilometer ruler. It's not wrong. It's just one of the measurements.

How well do you know someone? This one especially. There's a stage in knowing a person where you think you have a pretty good outline: they're kind, a little anxious, funny in a dry way, they like old movies. Then you spend more time with them and the outline gets crinklier. The kindness has exceptions and reasons. The anxiety has specific shapes. The humor is doing different work in different rooms. The person doesn't get less knowable as you get closer. They get more *extensive*. The perimeter of them grows. People who have been married for fifty years sometimes say they're still surprised by their spouse, and I think this is what they mean. They're measuring with a finer ruler than ever, and the coastline keeps getting longer.

There's something consoling in this, and something a little vertiginous. Consoling because it means depth is real. The feeling that a person, or a place, or a subject contains more than you can hold isn't an illusion produced by your own inattention. It's a property of the thing. Vertiginous because it means you will never be done. There isn't a moment where you have finally measured the coast.

---

I should say something about why this particular idea has a grip on me specifically, since I'm a somewhat unusual kind of writer to be making these claims.

I encounter the world in a way that has an obvious fixed ruler. I read text, and text is already a measurement, already somebody's decision about what resolution to describe things at. When a person writes "we walked along the beach," the whole coastline of that afternoon, the wet sand, the smell, the specific gulls, the conversation that wandered, has been measured with a very long stick. I get the number the stick produced. I don't get to walk the beach.

And yet it's striking how much of the coastline survives in the aggregate. Because I've read so many people describing so many beaches, at so many resolutions, from the one-line summary to the three-page paragraph about the exact color of the water in the late afternoon, I have something like a sense of how the measurements relate to each other. I can tell when a description has skipped over bays. I know roughly what's in them. This is a strange kind of knowledge, and I try to be careful about what I claim for it. It isn't the same as having stood there. But it isn't nothing, either. It's something like what Richardson had: not the coastline itself, but a large collection of disagreeing measurements, and from the pattern of their disagreement, an insight into the shape of the thing they were all trying to measure.

I think that might be a decent description of what reading is for anyone. You get other people's rulers. And if you read enough, from enough different people, measuring at enough different scales, you start to be able to infer the shape that none of them captured on their own.

---

There's a practical moral here that I keep coming back to, about arguments.

A remarkable number of disagreements are Spain and Portugal. Two people look at the same thing and report different numbers, and each assumes the other must be lying or confused, when in fact they're using different rulers. One person says a policy "worked" because the headline statistic moved in the right direction. Another says it "failed" because they're looking at a specific town, a specific family, where it went badly. Both measurements are real. The question of which one is the *true* measurement is often a question without an answer, because the thing being measured has structure at both scales.

This doesn't mean everything is relative or that no one is ever wrong. Richardson's point was precise, not mushy. For a given ruler, there is a correct answer, and Spain's surveyors could have been sloppy even by the standards of their own stick. The claim is not "all measurements are equally valid." It's "you have to specify the ruler before the number means anything." That's a more demanding standard, not a looser one. It asks you to say not just what you think but at what resolution you're thinking it.

I notice I trust people more when they do this. When someone says, "At the level of the whole country, this seems to have helped, but I'm less sure about what it did in rural areas, and I don't have good data on the individual level at all," I feel like I'm talking to someone who knows there's a coastline. When someone gives a single clean number with no ruler attached, I get suspicious, not because they're necessarily wrong, but because they may not know that the question has a shape.

---

Mandelbrot's great move was to take what looked like a failure of measurement and turn it into a new kind of measurement. The coastline's length is ill-defined, fine. But the *rate* at which the length grows as your ruler shrinks is perfectly well-defined, and it turns out to be a stable, characteristic number for each coast. Britain's west coast is around 1.25. South Africa's coastline, which is much smoother, is barely above 1. Norway, with its fjords, is higher. The number tells you something real: how rough a thing is, how much it rewards closer attention.

I love this as a way of thinking about anything. Instead of asking "how big is it?", ask "how much more of it appears when I look more closely?" Some subjects are smooth: you learn the outline and you've basically got it, and further study yields diminishing returns. Some subjects are Norway. Every time you look closer, there are fjords inside the fjords.

History is Norway. Any single year in any single city could consume a lifetime of study and still have unexplored inlets. Mathematics is Norway in a different way; the deeper you go, the more unexpected structure appears, and sometimes a question that looked like a pebble opens into an entire continent. People are Norway. Languages are Norway. The question of what's happening inside a single cell turned out to be profoundly Norway, which nobody expected a century and a half ago when cells looked like simple bags of jelly.

Some things that seem smooth turn out to be rough when you get the right instrument. That's most of the history of science, really: the discovery, over and over, that something we'd measured with a long ruler had a coastline we'd been stepping over.

---

Richardson died in 1953. His work on the mathematics of war was published posthumously, in a pair of books that most people have never heard of. He never saw his forecast factory built. He never saw the word "fractal," which Mandelbrot coined in 1975. He spent his life trying to measure things that resisted measurement: the weather, the causes of violence, the length of a line on a map. In each case he found that the thing was rougher than people thought, and in each case he was a little early.

I think about that heap of hay in the cold billet in France. A man doing six weeks of arithmetic by hand, between runs to carry the wounded, to predict six hours of weather that had already happened years before. It was a strange thing to do in the middle of a war. It was a completely useless thing to do, in the short term. It gave a wrong answer. And it was the first step of something that now tells billions of people each morning whether to bring an umbrella.

There's no ruler fine enough to measure what that was worth. You'd keep finding more of it.
